evidence: Caes. BG 7.62.2: cujus ductū saepe numerō hostēs superāssent
terms.comment: Mostly in the ablative, ductū alicujus, under someone’s leadership; in war the general’s command, often joined with auspicium (Lewis & Short). It also means a channel (ductus aquārum) and the stroke of a letter.

terms.grammar: ablative absolute of dux with a noun or pronoun: mē duce, tē duce
terms.comment: The commonest way to say “led by”: tē duce, with you leading (see leader).

terms.gloss: first place; the leadership of a people
evidence: Caes. BG 6.8.9: prīncipātus atque imperium est trāditum
terms.comment: First place among others, and so the leadership of a state or a people; under the emperors, the reign of the prīnceps (Lewis & Short).
Suetonius’ word for a command, and in Church Latin guidance: caecus autem sī caecō ducātum praestet (Vulg. Matt. 15.14).

phrases.latin: ipsum Caesarem, cujus ductū saepe numerō hostēs superāssent, praesentem adesse exīstimārent
phrases.english: (he told them) to imagine that Caesar himself, under whose leadership they had so often beaten the enemy, was there with them

phrases.latin: ac nē forte rogēs, quō mē duce, quō lare tūter
phrases.english: and in case you ask whose lead I follow, whose roof shelters me

phrases.latin: ut quisque aetāte antecēdit, ita sententiae prīncipātum tenet
phrases.english: whoever is ahead in age has the first say
